book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that The Good Place is unique among TV comedies in taking real moral philosophy seriously instead of playing the professor for a fool: Chidi Anagonye is a deontology-focused ethics professor whose 'mini ethics lessons' ground the plot, and philosophy becomes the vocabulary Eleanor and the others use to make sense of themselves. It recounts the show's premise (Eleanor waking in Michael's Neighborhood 12358W with Janet the 'vessel of all knowledge'), explains why a philosophy-professor character is rare on television, and sets out the volume's title conventions and spoiler warning.

chapters.file: ch10 - I The Demons in the Details.md
ch11 - 1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic.md
chapters.relation: Reads the show's automatic, unquestionable point system as Hannah Arendt's bureaucracy — 'rule by Nobody' in which no one, not Michael, not Shawn, not even Judge Gen, has authority over the system ('He's not God, he's a bureaucrat'). It argues via Arendt's power/violence distinction that bureaucracies deprive everyone subject to them of the power to act, leaving only resistance or violence, which is why Michael's Season Two plea before Gen ('the very method we use to deem them good or bad is fundamentally flawed') and his Season Three interference amount to revolt. Chidi's 'Most Improved Player' defense of Eleanor and Michael's case that souls can grow after death show the system cannot accommodate rehabilitation, only retribution.

chapters.file: ch12 - 2. How Can Torture Be This Funny.md
chapters.relation: Asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny and answers with incongruity theory (circus music under Michael's dejection; a comedy set in Hell) plus Bergson's view of comedy as social correction that deflates those who deserve it — Tahani's name-dropping, Michael failing 802 reboots. It centers on 'The Trolley Problem': Michael teleporting Chidi's ethics lesson into real runaway trolleys ('not real, but the pain is') is both incongruous humor and genuine torture, and invoking Bernard Williams shows the real wrongdoer is Michael, who rigged the situation, not Chidi who must choose. Eternal torture, it concludes, only works as endless low-grade everyday crappiness, which is comic in twenty-two-minute doses — and Eleanor's twice-given forgiveness of Michael, after seeing the centuries of torture in Janet's VR device, is the show's real moral marvel.

Argues, against Michael, that the Soul Squad still belongs in the Bad Place: drawing on William James's conditions for actions having moral worth (foreseeable consequences, no do-overs) and his meliorism about an unfinished, responsive universe, it shows the points system is contextualist (the tricycle fix worth +4.79 or +0.04; the two Dougs' rose gifts), but the afterlife simulation is a context where nothing the humans do is consequential or permanent, so their moral growth earns no points. Worse, their growth adds net unhappiness — Michael's suffering, the demon cast's misery, Judge Gen's distress — so becoming better ironically confirms they belong in the Bad Place. Only Michael, whose retirement is a real, irreversible consequence and whose sacrifices add genuine good, deserves the Good Place.

chapters.file: ch14 - 4. Can We Do Enough Good.md
chapters.relation: Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?

chapters.file: ch15 - 5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon.md
chapters.relation: Sets up the contradiction that the four humans must have free will to deserve punishment yet be predictable enough for Michael's torture to work, then tests compatibilism on Jason's snorkel death in the safe and Eleanor's confession — where it becomes unclear whether her guilt or Chidi's external 'moral quandary grimace' was decisive. Sartre's bad faith explains the humans' predictability: Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, Tahani's charity done for approval she won't admit to, and Trevor tempting Eleanor to identify as an 'Arizona trash bag' by nature. The chapter lands on determinism with complex, interacting causes (Eleanor not drinking at the party; Chidi's rare decisiveness), concluding the afterlife's real flaw is rewarding and punishing outcomes no one chose and that can serve no incentive function.

Asks whether Judge Gen could ever justly consign Team Cockroach to eternal torment. It reconstructs the Anselmian infinite-desert defense (God as 'than which none greater can be conceived', every sin against an infinite being meriting infinite punishment) and shows it fails on the show since no such God appears and neither Gen nor Michael is infinitely great; the continuing-sin model fails because the Bad Place's physical tortures (eyeball corkscrews, bees with teeth) preclude sinning, and Gen's own tests (Jason's Madden game, Tahani's hallway, Chidi's two hats) show vice persisting without added desert. Punishment as retribution also fails on utilitarian grounds (Jason's hypothetical spray-paint-can sentence adds only pain), so the chapter proposes a non-retributive 'Bad Place 3.0' where people face the natural consequences of their vices, comparing it to C.S. Lewis's The Great Divorce.

chapters.file: ch18 - 7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife.md
chapters.relation: Builds a dilemma from 'Existential Crisis': Michael's prospective retirement (via Todd May's Death) makes finitude look meaning-destroying, while the humans' endless existence — 802 reboots, Mindy St. Claire's eternal Cannonball Run II in the Medium Place — threatens boredom and disconnection from past selves. Testing God-free answers, it runs through Camus's Sisyphus, Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view, Susan Wolf's requirement that we love what deserves to be loved (Eleanor's philosophy study, friendship with Tahani, romance with Chidi), and John Martin Fischer on free authorship and narrative order (Eleanor's note to herself in What We Owe to Each Other). Conclusion: Eleanor and friends can lead meaningful lives even if damned and repeatedly rebooted.

chapters.file: ch19 - 8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning.md
chapters.relation: Reads Chidi's 'Jeremy Bearimy' breakdown — quoting Nietzsche's Parable of the Madman ('God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him') after learning he has been tortured for three hundred years — as the nihilism that follows the death of God, where the Judge's verdict that the humans seek only 'moral deserts' strips their moral project of purpose. Michael's post-crisis makeover party is Camus's embrace of the absurd (Sisyphus pushing the boulder), and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism supplies the way out: abandonment, anguish, and the French Soldier dilemma clarify Eleanor's confession in Season One and her lie that she failed the Judge's test as authentic choices. Once there is no hope of the Good Place, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake.

chapters.file: ch21 - 9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place.md
chapters.relation: Asks whether a show about ethics may lie to its audience for a whole season: the Season One twist breaks the viewer's implicit contract even though the show keeps its internal 'truth in fiction'. Through 'The Eternal Shriek' it stages the debate — Chidi's Kantian ban on lying (the red cowboy boots saga with Henry, ending in a confession that defeats Henry) against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means plot to 'kill' Janet — and reads the show's cascade of confessions as its answer that truth-telling absolves. Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' lets Chidi lie his way through Hell, leaving viewers to decide whether the twist's ethical education justifies the deception.

chapters.file: ch22 - 10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis.md
chapters.relation: Casts Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis in an allegorical love story: Chidi's Kantian universalizability about lying and his utilitarian lesson (confess, because the neighborhood's welfare outweighs you) only move Eleanor when she sees Theory enacted — Michael's willingness to absorb eternal torture in her place convinces her the theory 'has legs'. Praxis repays the debt when Eleanor's moral particularism pushes Chidi to lie to demons and play his part in the Bad Place party, and Michael's conversion from torturer to someone who sacrifices his portal pin for Eleanor ('Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent') completes the union. The moral: theory is born in the world, but only practice lets it thrive there.

Treats Chidi's indecision (rock-paper-scissors panic, the soul-mate dilemma, the boots lie) as the show's authentic portrait of how hard moral life is, not just a professor joke. Michael's live-action Trolley Problem — Foot's thought experiment made literal, with Henry's bloody boots flying at Chidi — is read as torture precisely because it weaponizes Chidi's defining trait, and the show pointedly never hands the audience a right answer. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired movies-vs-er argument ('Your boy Kant would say never break a promise') finally lets Chidi act, and Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other frames his arc's resolution: we choose to be good because of our bonds with others, as when he kisses Eleanor in 'Somewhere Else' and Michael 'solves' the trolley by sacrificing himself.

chapters.file: ch25 - 12. How the Fork Did I Get Here.md
chapters.relation: Asks what makes the person sitting in Michael's office numerically identical to the person who died on Earth. The same-body theory fails because bodies stay behind (buried or cremated) with no spatiotemporal continuity; the same-mind theory of psychological continuity fails on the 802 memory-wiping reboots and the duplication case of two psychologically-continuous Eleanors; the same-soul theory cannot say what makes two souls the same soul. The chapter concludes that 'Janet(s)' — essences reconstituting themselves in Janet's void — quietly commits the show to Aristotelian and Aquinan hylomorphism, while leaving open how anyone (even Janet) could tell that two persons share an essence.

chapters.file: ch26 - 13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts.md
chapters.relation: Uses the philosophy of divine omniscience (Aquinas's perfect knowledge, Averroes's self-knowing cause) to assess Janet's claim to know 'literally everything': on the all-true-propositions model she falls short — she misses Michael's deception, the future, and current events on Earth — which is a feature, since no foreknowledge means no threat to free will and no need for Boethius's eternal-present solution. Frank Jackson's Mary's room and Linda Zagzebski's omnisubjectivity frame Judge Gen's failure: 'You can't judge humans 'cause you don't know what we go through,' as Jason says, and her trip to Earth is her stepping out of the black-and-white room. Janet's gradual acquisition of experienced emotion — love for Jason, empathy for the Soul Squad — is likewise a kind of knowing no database contains.

chapters.file: ch27 - 14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors.md
chapters.relation: Defends Kant against the charge that he is why everyone hates moral philosophy professors: it explains the two-question Categorical Imperative test via frozen-yogurt maxims and Eleanor's selfish 'won't help unless it benefits me' principle, shows Kant never actually forbade lying to the murderer at the door (his crotchety 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' was an obscure legal point), and reads Chidi's trolley-track switch but refusal to harvest Eleanor's organs as the humanity formula — never treat a person merely as a means. Tahani's $60 billion in charity and Eleanor's failed point-chasing in 'What's My Motivation?' illustrate the good will: deeds lack moral worth unless done for the right reasons. Aristotle explains the residual puzzle — theory mastery does not make you skilled at ethical practice, any more than a nutritionist is a great cook.

Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.

Puts the show beside Sartre's No Exit, its acknowledged inspiration: Michael's neighborhood, like Garcin, Inez, and Estelle's drawing room, locks flawed people together to torture each other, but the four humans keep helping each other instead ('we improved each other, and the four of us became a team'). Against the standard reading, it uses Sartre's 1964 preface ('if relations with someone else are twisted... that other person can only be Hell'), the Being and Nothingness footnote about a 'radical conversion' from bad faith to authenticity, and his late remark that 'Heaven is each other' to argue the two works are compatible: other people are Hell only under dependence on their judgment — Season One Tahani's condition — while authentic relationships can succeed.

chapters.file: ch31 - 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place.md
chapters.relation: Frames the show's paradox — each person is responsible for her choices, yet her identity and choices are formed by her relationships — as Sartre's 'condemned to be free' colliding with relational autonomy, then reads each character through it. Eleanor's lifelong rejection of dependence (emancipation, bringing her own birthday cake) kills her and only unwinds through Team Cockroach; Chidi's indecision is named as bad faith that ends under an air conditioner; Tahani, defined by others' approval, is crushed pulling down Kamilah's statue yet confronts her parents in the Judge's test; Jason's blind loyalty to Pillboi and Donkey Doug shows dependence unexamined. The lesson: embrace both accountability and dependence by choosing whom you let close.

chapters.file: ch32 - VI The Leap to Faith.md

chapters.relation: Treats the show as a theological sitcom whose afterlife (Gen's algorithmic judgment, cubicles, the Jeremy Bearimy timeline) critiques a pop-Christian eschatology of disembodied Heaven and eternal conscious torment while missing the bodily resurrection of Nicene and N.T. Wright's account. Levinas supplies the positive frame: ethics precedes ontology, the face of the Other demands responsibility before any impersonal verdict — which is why Gen's points system 'wouldn't cut it' and why the show's two-shots, Eleanor's spontaneous good acts, and Chidi's 802 yeses to teaching her matter. Bonhoeffer's religionless Christianity completes the reading of Eleanor's repentance, Donna's and Tahani's confessions, and Michael's self-sacrificing Christ figure: salvation comes through intersubjective, grace-infused transformation, so 'Heaven is other people'.

chapters.file: ch34 - 19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right.md
chapters.relation: Argues Hinduism 'gets more than five percent right' via the Bhagavad Gita: the show's point system mirrors karma, Eleanor's failed point-chasing and quiet departure for the Bad Place enact nishkama karma (desire-less action), and the 802 reboots are rebirths without memory. The characters form a ladder of unfoldment — Jason's unknowing wrong action below Eleanor's knowing one, Tahani's corruptly motivated good deeds, Chidi's knowledge without decision, Michael swerving from his demonic dharma, and Janet highest: desireless, rebooting like cyclical rebirth, her void echoing boundless Brahman. Chidi's logic-bound indecision versus Eleanor's knowledge-producing logic completes the Gita reading.

A health warning from Jonathan Dancy himself: the show's premise that Chidi's lessons in Kant, Scanlon, and the Trolley Problem can make Eleanor better is false, because becoming good requires a change in motivation and intellectual study shapes motivation at most indirectly — and might attach to the wrong as easily as the right, since moral philosophy studies both. Worse, studying ethics looks like self-indulgence, time spent on Kant that could have gone to doing actual good. Against the Kantian thought that only acting from a sense of duty earns moral credit, Dancy argues that sympathetic love — Doug Wynegar bringing his grandmother roses simply for her sake — is enough, which undermines both Kant and Chidi's entire teaching project.

chapters.file: ch37 - 21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good.md
chapters.relation: Argues that no one can improve without first admitting they are bad: the rigid Good Place/Bad Place binary is ethical dualism whose cracks show in Mindy St. Claire's Medium Place and Jason, a naive moral neutral who fits neither side. Socrates' Apology supplies the method — wisdom is knowing what you do not know, so self-aware fault-finding precedes growth — while Aristotle's account of virtue as learned by practice, like an instrument, grounds the claim that goodness can be acquired even in the afterlife, though unlearning old habits is harder. Eleanor's trash storm, Tahani's failed party, and Chidi's theory-practice gap mark each character's admissions of error, and the worst offenders, Eleanor and Michael, improve most because they confess unprompted.

Brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings are evolved, body-based shortcuts built from a lifetime of social interaction that prune options in real-time moral choice, so Chidi's classroom mastery paired with real-world collapse mirrors Damasio's ventromedial patients — except Chidi has the alarms and refuses to trust them, insisting ethics is pure calculation. Mark Johnson's moral imagination (his own draft-number dilemma) and Scanlon's contractualism (morality is other people) reinforce that we are not disembodied reasoners. Combining Dewey's 'morals is education' with Damasio's claim that somatic learning never stops, the chapter explains how Eleanor and friends keep growing morally even after death — bodies, social bonds and all.

chapters.file: ch39 - 23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness.md
chapters.relation: Begins with Schur's traffic-light story — the fourth car sneaking through the left-turn arrow as 'negative twenty points' — to argue the show is, before it is about ethics, an attack on selfish inauthenticity: Tahani's name-dropping charity, Eleanor's lunch-table declaration of friendlessness, Chidi's moral filibustering, and Jason's Acidcat gig each pursue a self at others' expense. Using Charles Guignon's On Being Authentic and Kant's language of means and ends, it traces the movement from authenticity that uses others to an authenticity that lives for others — Chidi's 802 unconditional yeses, Michael's shift from torturer to self-sacrificer to paralyzed would-be hero, and Eleanor giving up Chidi in 'Pandemonium' as the endpoint. Being true to yourself, the show teaches, is only ethical when it helps others be their truest selves.

holes.name: Rule by Nobody (bureaucracy)
holes.what: Arendt's account of bureaucracy as a system in which no one can be held responsible — 'rule by Nobody', the most tyrannical form since there is no one to answer — which deprives everyone of power and breeds violence as the only recourse.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire argument reads the afterlife's automatic point system, and Michael's and Gen's powerlessness before it, through this Arendtian concept.

holes.name: Meliorism
holes.what: William James's doctrine that the world is unfinished and plastic, so individual and collective effort can genuinely improve it — with the added conditions that actions must have foreseeable consequences and be irreversible to carry moral worth.
holes.why: Chapter 13 uses James's meliorism and its two conditions to argue the humans' post-death growth earns no points, while Michael's irreversible sacrifices do.

holes.name: Infinite Desert of Sin (why Hell is eternal)
holes.what: The Anselmian defense of eternal punishment: because God is an infinitely great being and every sin is against God, any wrongdoing, however small, deserves infinite punishment.
holes.why: Chapter 17's central question — whether Judge Gen can justly impose eternal torture — is structured around testing this doctrine and its three claims (INFINITE, SIN, GREATER).

holes.name: Moral Particularism
holes.what: The view, associated with Jonathan Dancy, that there are no invariant moral principles: what one ought to do is determined case by case by the morally relevant particulars of the situation.
holes.why: Chapters 21, 22, and 23 pivot on Eleanor citing Dancy's particularism to overturn Chidi's Kantian ban on lying so the Soul Squad can escape the Bad Place.

holes.name: Jonathan Dancy
holes.what: Contemporary British moral philosopher, professor at the University of Texas at Austin, best known as the leading defender of moral particularism.
holes.why: The show's recurring 'movies vs. ER' argument is attributed to him by name, he authors chapter 36 of this very volume, and his particularism resolves the lying dilemma in chapters 21-23.

holes.name: Contractualism (What We Owe to Each Other)
holes.what: T.M. Scanlon's view that an act is wrong if it would be disallowed by principles no one could reasonably reject, grounding morality in what we owe one another through our bonds with other people.
holes.why: The book on which Eleanor writes her note is the show's touchstone (chapters 23, 30, 38, 39 all lean on it), and Chidi's closing lecture — we choose to be good because of our bonds with others — is Scanlon's answer.

holes.name: Omniscience (as a divine attribute)
holes.what: The doctrine that a perfect being knows all true propositions, traditionally counted among God's defining attributes and complicated by foreknowledge and by whether propositional knowledge exhausts understanding.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies the philosophical analysis of omniscience point by point to decide whether Janet is really all-knowing and what her gaps mean.

holes.name: Three Independent Factors in Morals
holes.what: Dewey's essay arguing that the Good (desire), the Right (socially authorized demand), and the Virtuous (social praise and blame) are irreducible factors in moral experience, so genuine moral conflict and uncertainty are inescapable.
holes.why: Chapter 28's critique of the Big Three and its reading of Eleanor's 'option C' and the Medium Place as Deweyan reconciliation rest on this specific theory, not covered by the taxonomy's Dewey entries.

holes.name: Relational Autonomy
holes.what: The feminist idea that persons are socially constituted: autonomy is formed, exercised, and constrained through relationships with others rather than in spite of them.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explicitly names relational autonomy as one of the two traditions behind its paradox of individual accountability versus social dependence.

holes.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
holes.what: German Lutheran pastor-theologian executed by the Nazis in 1945, known for his prison-era 'religionless Christianity' and an ethics of responsibility modeled on Christ's example.
holes.why: Chapter 33 devotes a full section to reading Eleanor's repentance arc and Michael's self-sacrifice as Bonhoefferian responsible action, alongside Levinas.

holes.name: Eschatology (doctrine of last things)
holes.what: The theological study of death, judgment, Heaven and Hell, and the final destiny of creation, including competing Christian accounts such as eternal conscious torment, universalism, and annihilationism.
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues the show both critiques and imperfectly reproduces Christian eschatology, which is its central analytical frame.

holes.name: Nishkama Karma (desire-less action)
holes.what: The Bhagavad Gita's teaching that one should perform one's duty without desire for the fruits of the action, since corrupt motivation strips an act of worth.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads Eleanor's failed point-chasing and her selfless departure as exactly this Gita doctrine, the linchpin of its Hindu reading of the show.

holes.name: Karma and Rebirth (Hindu)
holes.what: The Hindu doctrine, central to the Bhagavad Gita, that actions determine consequences across cycles of birth, death, and rebirth until self-realization frees one from the cycle.
holes.why: Chapter 34 maps the show's point system onto karma and the 802 reboots (Janet's included) onto rebirth; the taxonomy's only karma slug is Buddhist-attributed, which would misrepresent this explicitly Hindu chapter.

holes.name: Somatic Marker Hypothesis
holes.what: Antonio Damasio's neuroscience thesis that bodily 'gut feelings' bias and prune decision options, making emotion integral to rational moral choice rather than its enemy.
holes.why: Chapter 38 explains Chidi's stomachaches through this hypothesis and uses it to attack the rationalist split between emotion and reasoning in traditional moral theory.
